questions.q: What is the "entered currency amount" on a foreign currency journal line?
options: The amount converted to the ledger's functional currency
The amount as it actually occurred, in the original real-world transaction currency
A budgeted amount for comparison purposes only
The amount after year-end close adjustments
questions.explain: The entered amount preserves the real-world transaction exactly as it happened, in its original currency.

questions.q: Which amount actually updates the ledger's functional-currency balances, feeding trial balances and reports?
questions.explain: The accounted amount, converted to the ledger's functional currency, is what drives every balance, inquiry, and report.

questions.q: What does a conversion rate type like "Corporate" or "Spot" determine?
options: Which chart of accounts segment is used
The source of the exchange rate used to convert the entered amount into the accounted amount
questions.explain: The rate type selects which exchange rate source (e.g., a company-defined Corporate rate or actual market Spot rate) is used for conversion.

questions.q: In the worked example, LTV Manufacturing Corporation enters a GBP invoice of 8,500.00 at a Corporate rate of 1.27 USD/GBP. What is the accounted USD amount?
questions.explain: 8,500.00 x 1.27 = 10,795.00, which is the accounted amount that posts to the USD ledger.

questions.q: Why can an accounted amount booked at entry become inaccurate if the related balance is still outstanding at period end?
options: Because Oracle Fusion deletes old conversion rates automatically
Because the exchange rate may have moved since the journal was entered, changing the true functional-currency value of the still-open balance
Because entered currency amounts expire after 30 days
Because accounted amounts are always estimates, never exact
questions.explain: If the exchange rate moves after entry and the balance is still open, the originally accounted amount no longer reflects current value — the problem period-end revaluation addresses.
